KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

The center of the developing nor'easter is currently located 
due east of the Carolinas with a low-level circulation seen very
well on latest visible satellite. The nor'easter is forecast to
slowly lift northward and deepen through tonight and Saturday 
before stalling out and meandering south of southern New England
toward the Mid-Atlantic coast through the weekend. 

Even with a slower trend moving north, winds and seas have 
already started to respond to the tightening pressure gradient 
with the last Jeffrey's Ledge buoy observation coming in with 
just under 12 ft wave height as of 2 PM. Surf conditions will 
further deteriorate and remain dangerous through at least the 
weekend as swells and the long fetch of brisk northeast winds 
continue to build seas over the Gulf of Maine. The High Surf 
Advisory lasts through the day Sunday for large breaking waves 
and a high risk for rip currents, and there are indications that
these conditions may last through Monday with the nor'easter
slowing its departure. So it's possible a High Surf Advisory or
Rip Current Statement will be needed on Monday.

We're also entering into high astronomical tides, and the long-
duration of brisk northeast winds and 1-2' of storm surge will bring 
the potential for minor coastal flooding and splash-over. This is 
more likely for coastal York and coastal Rockingham counties where 
minor coastal flooding/beach erosion will be possible over multiple 
high tide cycles over the weekend as the northeast winds continue to 
push water toward the coastline. A Coastal Flood Advisory has been 
issued to cover this potential for coastal York/Rockingham from 
Saturday morning through late Sunday evening.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

The trend has continued for the nor'easter to slow it's progression 
north as dry high pressure to the north wins out. The low will stall 
out off the Mid-Atlantic coast Saturday and Sunday before finally 
moving up the coast and out to see at the beginning of the next work 
week.

Our area will be under a decent pressure gradient with high pressure 
to the north and the nor'easter to our south but the threat for 
stronger winds may have backed off just a bit as the low continues 
to trend further south. Forecast soundings at Portsmouth still 
suggest we could see some winds in the 40 to 45 knot range at the 
top of the mixed layer across southeast New Hampshire late Saturday 
through Sunday morning but available momentum should decreasing 
north and east. In general, it appears that the strongest gusts will 
be over portions of southeastern New Hampshire and southwest Maine 
to around 40 mph. Elsewhere expect breezy northeast winds gusting 25 
to 35 mph. While winds will not be overly strong, this will be a 
rather long duration event with winds increasing late tonight and 
potentially lasting into next week. Thus, with plenty of leaves on 
the trees there could be a limited power outage threat, especially 
along the coast and portions of the interior. 

The trend south will also impact the precipitation forecast. While 
we are still expecting a beneficial soaking rainfall for much of the 
southern and coastal areas, rainfall chances may not really start to 
increase until Saturday with the best chances now on Sunday and 
Monday. As the nor'easter stalls out off the Mid-Atlantic coast, 
rainfall will be slow to progress north so many areas may just 
experience a dry and breezy Saturday with a rainier end to the 
weekend. NBM probabilities suggest a 70 to 90 percent chance for 
least an inch of rain over southern New Hampshire and 
southwest/coastal Maine through Monday. The probabilities for at 
least 2 inches over the same time-frame are maximized over 
southeastern New Hampshire and far southwest Maine (50 to 80 
percent). Thus, it seems like a good bet that we will see some 
widespread totals in the 1 to 2 inch range with some locally higher 
amounts over southeast New Hampshire and/or far southwest Maine.  

The upper low moves overhead on Tuesday, so we may see some 
lingering precipitation chances before it finally kicks out of the 
region Tuesday night. Mean ridging will then move in mid to late 
week with highs pushing back into the 70s. While this time period 
looks mostly dry, a quick moving front could lead to some low 
precipitation chances late week.
